title: Aggregate and custom reductions
summary: All three Aggregate overloads, running totals done safely, building strings, and folding several results in one pass.

steps.title: Three Aggregates
body: Module 6 showed `Aggregate(seed, func)`. There are three versions:
```csharp
// 1. No seed: the FIRST item is the starting value
words.Aggregate((acc, w) => acc + "," + w)
// 2. A seed: start from this value
words.Aggregate(0, (n, w) => n + w.Length)
// 3. A seed and a result selector: convert the final value at the end
words.Aggregate("", (acc, w) => acc + w[0], acc => acc.ToUpper())
Every one is the same loop:
```csharp
var acc = seed;                 // or the first item
foreach (var x in items)        // or the remaining items
acc = func(acc, x);
return resultSelector(acc);
The accumulator can be **any type**: a number, a string, a tuple, even a list. That is what makes `Aggregate` the general tool behind `Sum`, `Max`, `string.Join` and friends.

code: Console.WriteLine(words.Aggregate("", (acc, w) => acc + w[0], acc => acc.ToUpper()));
steps.explain: With no seed, `acc` starts as `"one"`, then each new word goes in front: the words come out reversed. The seeded one adds lengths 3 + 3 + 5. The third collects first letters, `"ott"`, and the result selector upper-cases it at the end.

steps.prompt: `empty` is an `int[]` with no items. What happens?
code: int a = empty.Aggregate(0, (acc, n) => acc + n);
int b = empty.Aggregate((acc, n) => acc + n);
options: `a` is `0`, and the second line throws `InvalidOperationException`
`a` is `0` and `b` is `default`, also `0`, but a warning is printed
steps.explain: With a seed, an empty sequence simply returns the seed. Without one there is no first item to start from, so it throws. Prefer the seeded version unless the sequence can never be empty.

steps.title: Running totals
body: "The balance after each transaction" is a **running total**: one output per input, not one value at the end.
A tempting shortcut is a `Select` that updates a variable outside the lambda:
```csharp
int balance = 0;
var running = deposits.Select(d => balance += d);   // careful!
It works the first time. But the query is lazy (module 6): every enumeration runs the lambda **again**, and `balance` is not reset. Safer options:
```csharp
// Aggregate into a list: runs exactly once, nothing outside changes
var running = deposits.Aggregate(new List<int>(), (list, d) =>
list.Add((list.Count == 0 ? 0 : list[^1]) + d);
return list;
or a small `yield return` operator, which you will write in lesson 8.

steps.prompt: The shortcut, enumerated twice. What does this print?
steps.explain: The second `string.Join` runs the lambda again, starting from the `35` left over from the first run. A lambda with a side effect makes a query give a different answer each time you look at it.

steps.title: Building strings
body: Adding strings with `+` in a loop copies the whole string every time. For long output, use a `StringBuilder` as the seed and convert it once at the end with the **result selector**:
```csharp
string receipt = items.Aggregate(
new StringBuilder(),
(sb, item) => sb.Append(item.Name).Append(": ").Append(item.Price).Append('\n'),
sb => sb.ToString());
`Append` returns the same `StringBuilder`, so the lambda can chain calls and return it.
> **Tip:** if you only need separators between items, `string.Join(", ", items)` is clearer. Reach for `Aggregate` when each piece needs real work.

steps.prompt: Complete the line so `csv` becomes `"a;b;c;"` for the rows `a`, `b`, `c`.
steps.code: string csv = rows.Aggregate(new StringBuilder(), (sb, r) => sb.__1__(r).Append(';'), sb => sb.__2__());
steps.explain: `Append` adds to the builder and returns it. The result selector turns the finished builder into a string once.

steps.title: Min, max and count in one pass
prompt: Calling `Min()`, `Max()` and `Count()` walks the list three times. Write `static (int Min, int Max, int Count) Stats(List<int> xs)` that walks it **once** with a single `Aggregate` whose accumulator is a tuple.
- an empty list gives `(0, 0, 0)` (use the result selector for that)
Do not call `Min`, `Max` or `Count` on the list. `Math.Min` and `Math.Max` are fine.
starter: static (int Min, int Max, int Count) Stats(List<int> xs)
solution: static (int Min, int Max, int Count) Stats(List<int> xs)
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("Stats([4, 9, 2])", (2, 9, 3), Stats(new List<int> { 4, 9, 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("Stats with negatives", (-5, 7, 4), Stats(new List<int> { 0, -5, 7, 1 }));
Dojo.Eq("Stats of one item", (6, 6, 1), Stats(new List<int> { 6 }));
Dojo.Eq("Stats of nothing", (0, 0, 0), Stats(new List<int>()));

forbid.message: Does not call Min, Max or Count

hints: Seed: `(Min: int.MaxValue, Max: int.MinValue, Count: 0)`. Anything is smaller than `int.MaxValue`.
Step: `(acc, x) => (Math.Min(acc.Min, x), Math.Max(acc.Max, x), acc.Count + 1)`.

steps.title: Bank balance
prompt: An account opens with `opening`, then each value in `moves` is added (negative values are withdrawals). Write two methods, no loops:
- `static List<decimal> RunningBalance(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)`: the balance after each move. `RunningBalance(100, [-30, 50, -90])` is `[70, 120, 30]`.
- `static decimal Lowest(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)`: the lowest balance the account ever had, counting the opening. For the example: `30`. With no moves: `opening`.
Do not use a `Select` that changes a variable outside it.
starter: static List<decimal> RunningBalance(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)
static decimal Lowest(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)
solution: static List<decimal> RunningBalance(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)
static decimal Lowest(decimal opening, List<decimal> moves)
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoMoves = new List<decimal> { -30m, 50m, -90m };
Dojo.Eq("RunningBalance(100, [-30, 50, -90])", new List<decimal> { 70m, 120m, 30m }, RunningBalance(100m, dojoMoves));
Dojo.Eq("calling it twice gives the same answer", new List<decimal> { 70m, 120m, 30m }, RunningBalance(100m, dojoMoves));
Dojo.Eq("no moves", new List<decimal>(), RunningBalance(5m, new List<decimal>()));
Dojo.Eq("Lowest is 30", 30m, Lowest(100m, dojoMoves));
Dojo.Eq("Lowest can be the opening", 10m, Lowest(10m, new List<decimal> { 5m, 1m }));
Dojo.Eq("Lowest with an overdraft", -15m, Lowest(10m, new List<decimal> { -25m, 40m }));
hints: Seed `Aggregate` with `new List<decimal>()` and add one balance per move.
The previous balance is `list[^1]`, or `opening` while the list is still empty.
For `Lowest`, fold the balances with `Aggregate(opening, Math.Min)`, or `Prepend(opening).Min()`.

steps.title: Loop to Aggregate: longest streak
steps.prompt: `days[i]` is `true` if you practised on day `i`. This loop finds your longest run of practice days in a row. Rewrite it as **one `Aggregate`** with a tuple accumulator `(Current, Best)` and a result selector. No loops.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("T T F T T T F is 3", 3, LongestStreak(new List<bool> { true, true, false, true, true, true, false }));
Dojo.Eq("all false is 0", 0, LongestStreak(new List<bool> { false, false }));
Dojo.Eq("all true is the length", 4, LongestStreak(new List<bool> { true, true, true, true }));
Dojo.Eq("no days is 0", 0, LongestStreak(new List<bool>()));
hints: The two loop variables become the two parts of the tuple: seed `(Current: 0, Best: 0)`.
The loop body becomes the lambda: compute the new current, then return `(current, Math.Max(acc.Best, current))`.
`return best;` becomes the result selector `acc => acc.Best`.

steps.title: Sidekick: your streak
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** The dashboard says *Streak: 6 days in a row.* A streak counts **workdays**: logging on Friday and then on Monday keeps it going. The rule for weekends: **Saturday and Sunday are ignored**. Logging on a weekend neither adds to a streak nor breaks it (Sidekick tracks a working habit, and nobody should be punished for resting or rewarded for working through the weekend). Two methods:

`static int LongestStreak(IEnumerable<DateOnly> activeDays)`: drop the weekend days, then one `Aggregate` over the distinct days in order, with a tuple accumulator `(Best, Run, Last)` where `Last` is a `DateOnly?`. A day continues the run when `Sk.PreviousWorkday(day) == Last` (your piece from Robust code: Monday's previous workday is Friday). Empty: `0`.

`static int CurrentStreak(IEnumerable<DateOnly> activeDays, DateOnly today)`: the run that ends today, or ends at the previous workday if you have not logged anything yet today (or today is a weekend day). Walk back with `Sk.PreviousWorkday` through a `HashSet` of the workdays.

Examples: active Mon 16 to Fri 20 Nov, Mon 23, Tue 24, then Thu 26: the longest streak is 7. Active Fri 20, Sat 21, Mon 23, Tue 24: the longest is 3 (Saturday is skipped, not a break). Only Sat 21 and Sun 22: 0.
starter: static int CurrentStreak(IEnumerable<DateOnly> activeDays, DateOnly today) => 0;
solution: int run = acc.Last is DateOnly last && Sk.PreviousWorkday(day) == last ? acc.Run + 1 : 1;
static int CurrentStreak(IEnumerable<DateOnly> activeDays, DateOnly today)
var days = activeDays.Where(d => d.DayOfWeek is not (DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday)).ToHashSet();
template: {{CODE}}
DateOnly DojoNov(int d) => new DateOnly(2026, 11, d);
var dojoDays = new List<DateOnly> { DojoNov(26), DojoNov(17), DojoNov(16), DojoNov(18), DojoNov(19), DojoNov(20), DojoNov(23), DojoNov(24), DojoNov(17) };
Dojo.Eq("longest: Mon 16 to Tue 24 over the weekend", 7, LongestStreak(dojoDays));
Dojo.Eq("a missed Wednesday breaks the run", 2, LongestStreak(new[] { DojoNov(24), DojoNov(26), DojoNov(27) }));
Dojo.Eq("one day", 1, LongestStreak(new[] { DojoNov(3) }));
Dojo.Eq("no days", 0, LongestStreak(new List<DateOnly>()));
Dojo.Eq("current: nothing yet today, counted from yesterday", 7, CurrentStreak(dojoDays.Where(d => d != DojoNov(26)), DojoNov(25)));
Dojo.Eq("current: today counts", 1, CurrentStreak(dojoDays, DojoNov(26)));
Dojo.Eq("current on a Monday reaches back to Friday", 6, CurrentStreak(dojoDays.Where(d => d < DojoNov(24)), DojoNov(23)));
Dojo.Eq("current: a gap means 0", 0, CurrentStreak(dojoDays, DojoNov(30)));
Dojo.Eq("a Saturday in between is skipped, not a break", 3, LongestStreak(new[] { DojoNov(20), DojoNov(21), DojoNov(23), DojoNov(24) }));
Dojo.Eq("weekend-only activity is no streak", 0, LongestStreak(new[] { DojoNov(21), DojoNov(22) }));
Dojo.Eq("current on a Sunday counts back from Friday", 2, CurrentStreak(new[] { DojoNov(19), DojoNov(20), DojoNov(22) }, DojoNov(22)));
Dojo.Eq("current: weekend work after Friday still counts Friday", 3, CurrentStreak(new[] { DojoNov(19), DojoNov(20), DojoNov(21), DojoNov(23) }, DojoNov(23)));
static partial class Sk
internal static DateOnly PreviousWorkday(DateOnly day) => day.DayOfWeek switch
DayOfWeek.Monday => day.AddDays(-3),
DayOfWeek.Sunday => day.AddDays(-2),
_ => day.AddDays(-1),
hints: Start with `.Where(day => day.DayOfWeek is not (DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday))`, then `Distinct().Order()`.
In the lambda: `acc.Last is DateOnly last && Sk.PreviousWorkday(day) == last` decides whether the run continues.
CurrentStreak: filter the weekends into a `HashSet`, start at today if it is in the set, otherwise at `Sk.PreviousWorkday(today)`.
steps.explain: The tuple accumulator carries exactly the state the loop version kept in three variables. Reusing `PreviousWorkday` means the weekend rule lives in one place in your Sidekick.
